params.question: According to the neonatal classification system, which birth weight cut-off defines very low birth weight (VLBW)?

answers.text: Less than 2,500 grams

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This defines low birth weight (LBW), the broader category. VLBW uses a lower threshold of 1,500 grams.

answers.text: Less than 1,500 grams

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. VLBW is defined as under 1,500 grams, sitting between LBW (<2,500 g) and ELBW (<1,000 g) in the birth weight classification.

answers.text: Less than 1,000 grams

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This defines extremely low birth weight (ELBW), the most severe category. VLBW is the intermediate threshold at under 1,500 grams.

answers.text: Less than 2,000 grams

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: There is no standard neonatal classification at 2,000 grams. The recognised thresholds are 2,500 g (LBW), 1,500 g (VLBW), and 1,000 g (ELBW).

overallFeedback.feedback: VLBW is defined as birth weight under 1,500 grams. Remember the three-step classification: LBW (<2,500 g), VLBW (<1,500 g), and ELBW (<1,000 g).

Well done. The birth weight classification uses three key thresholds: LBW (<2,500 g), VLBW (<1,500 g), and ELBW (<1,000 g). Each sub-group carries progressively higher risks for survival and complications.

interactions.label: Why does the foramen ovale close within minutes of birth?

params.question: Why does the foramen ovale close within minutes of birth?

answers.text: Rising oxygen levels directly cause the septal flap to constrict

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Rising oxygen primarily constricts the ductus arteriosus, not the foramen ovale. The foramen ovale closes through a different mechanism involving pressure changes between the atria.

answers.text: The first breaths reduce pulmonary resistance while cord clamping raises systemic resistance, reversing the pressure gradient across the atria

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Lung expansion drops pulmonary vascular resistance, increasing left atrial pressure, while cord clamping raises systemic resistance. This pressure reversal pushes the septal flap shut against the atrial septum.

answers.text: Surfactant release triggers a hormonal cascade that seals the foramen

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Surfactant prevents alveolar collapse and aids gas exchange, but plays no direct role in closing the foramen ovale. Closure is driven by the pressure reversal between the two atria.

answers.text: Cessation of umbilical venous flow removes the blood that kept the foramen patent

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While cord clamping does stop umbilical venous flow, the foramen ovale closes specifically because left atrial pressure exceeds right atrial pressure after the first breaths expand the lungs and drop pulmonary resistance.

overallFeedback.feedback: The foramen ovale closes because the baby's first breaths reduce pulmonary resistance (raising left atrial pressure) while cord clamping raises systemic resistance. This pressure reversal pushes the septal flap shut. Remember: foramen ovale = pressure, ductus arteriosus = oxygen.

Exactly. The pressure reversal — lung expansion dropping pulmonary resistance and cord clamping raising systemic resistance — closes the foramen ovale. The ductus arteriosus, by contrast, constricts in response to rising oxygen levels.

interactions.label: A 2-minute-old baby has a heart rate of 45 bpm despite 30 seconds of effective p

params.question: A 2-minute-old baby has a heart rate of 45 bpm despite 30 seconds of effective positive pressure ventilation with visible chest rise. You begin chest compressions using the two-thumb encircling method. After 60 seconds of compressions and ventilation, the heart rate is still 50 bpm. What is the most appropriate next step?

answers.text: Switch to the two-finger compression technique for better chest recoil

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The two-thumb encircling method actually generates higher coronary perfusion pressure than the two-finger method. Switching to a less effective technique would not improve the outcome.

answers.text: Increase the compression rate to 120 per minute

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The neonatal standard is 90 compressions coordinated with 30 breaths per minute in a 3:1 ratio. Simply increasing rate without addressing the underlying hypoxia will not restore circulation.

answers.text: Administer epinephrine

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. When the heart rate remains below 60 bpm after a full minute of effective compressions and ventilation, epinephrine is the next step in the neonatal resuscitation algorithm.

answers.text: Stop compressions and perform only bag-mask ventilation at a higher rate

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Effective ventilation is already confirmed by visible chest rise. Stopping compressions when the heart rate is critically low would remove circulatory support. The correct escalation at this point is to add epinephrine.

overallFeedback.feedback: When the heart rate remains below 60 bpm despite 60 seconds of effective chest compressions and ventilation, the next step is epinephrine. Remember the escalation sequence: ventilation → compressions → medication.

Well done. The neonatal resuscitation algorithm follows a clear escalation: effective ventilation first, then chest compressions if HR stays below 60, then epinephrine if HR remains below 60 after one minute of combined compressions and ventilation.

interactions.label: A 34-week preterm baby born 4 hours ago shows moderate encephalopathy following

params.question: A 34-week preterm baby born 4 hours ago shows moderate encephalopathy following birth asphyxia. Is this baby eligible for therapeutic hypothermia?

answers.text: Yes, because moderate encephalopathy and presentation within 6 hours meet the criteria

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Moderate encephalopathy and being within 6 hours satisfy only two of the three required criteria. The baby must also be at least 36 weeks gestation to qualify.

answers.text: Yes, because any baby with birth asphyxia and encephalopathy should receive cooling

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Therapeutic hypothermia is not indicated for all asphyxiated babies. The evidence supporting cooling comes from studies on term and near-term neonates, and all three eligibility criteria must be met.

answers.text: No, because the baby's gestational age is below the 36-week threshold

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Therapeutic hypothermia requires all three criteria: gestational age ≥36 weeks, moderate or severe encephalopathy, and presentation within 6 hours of birth. At 34 weeks, this baby does not qualify.

answers.text: No, because therapeutic hypothermia must be started within 2 hours of birth

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The time window for initiating therapeutic hypothermia is 6 hours, not 2 hours. This baby is within the time window but fails on the gestational age criterion.

overallFeedback.feedback: Therapeutic hypothermia has three strict eligibility criteria: gestational age ≥36 weeks, moderate or severe encephalopathy, and presentation within 6 hours of birth. This baby fails the gestational age criterion at 34 weeks.
Exactly. All three eligibility criteria — gestational age ≥36 weeks, moderate or severe encephalopathy, and presentation within 6 hours — must be met before cooling a baby to 33–34 °C for 72 hours.

interactions.label: A growth-restricted (IUGR) term baby typically presents with thin, translucent s

params.question: A growth-restricted (IUGR) term baby typically presents with thin, translucent skin, soft flat ears, and poor muscle tone.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: Those features — thin translucent skin, soft flat ears, and poor muscle tone — are hallmarks of a preterm baby, reflecting organ immaturity. A growth-restricted term baby shows loose, dry, wrinkled skin, disproportionate head-sparing, and is typically alert despite being underweight.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — this statement is false. Thin, translucent skin, soft ears, and poor tone are signs of prematurity (organ immaturity). A growth-restricted baby instead has loose, dry, wrinkled skin, a head that looks relatively large compared to a wasted body (head-sparing), and is often surprisingly alert and hungry.

interactions.label: A newborn delivered by forceps after prolonged labour is not moving the right ar

params.question: A newborn delivered by forceps after prolonged labour is not moving the right arm spontaneously. Both clavicles feel normal on palpation and there is no visible swelling over the arm. Which category of birth injury is most likely?

answers.text: Soft tissue injury

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Soft tissue injuries present with visible swelling, bruising, or abrasions over the affected area, usually right over the presenting part. The absence of any swelling in this case makes soft tissue injury unlikely.

answers.text: Skeletal injury

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While fractures can cause pseudo-paralysis, normal clavicular palpation and absence of swelling or crepitus make a skeletal injury less likely in this scenario.

answers.text: Nerve injury

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Absent spontaneous movement of one arm without swelling or bony abnormality strongly suggests a brachial plexus injury. Nerve injuries characteristically produce asymmetry — one limb not moving — and are common after instrumental delivery and prolonged labour.

answers.text: Visceral injury

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Visceral injuries typically present hours after birth with pallor, abdominal distension, and cardiovascular instability. They do not cause isolated limb immobility.

overallFeedback.feedback: When a newborn fails to move one arm without visible swelling or bony crepitus, think nerve injury — specifically brachial plexus injury. The pattern-matching rule: soft tissue = swelling, skeletal = crepitus or deformity, nerve = asymmetry, visceral = delayed systemic signs.

Well done. In birth injuries, asymmetric limb movement without visible swelling or bony abnormality points to nerve injury — most commonly brachial plexus injury after instrumental or prolonged delivery.
